title: The Whole Vow
premise: Noor Ishikawa has spent ten years ghostwriting other people's truths, including the memoir of his old rival and former best friend, Elias Vane. When a shared inheritance forces both their names onto the deed of a failing family orchard in Hokkaido-adjacent Vermont, Noor must confront the confession he abandoned a decade ago: that he loved Elias, and left to protect a friendship he thought he'd already ruined. As harvest festival deadlines collide with the memoir's publication, Noor learns Elias has known about the ghostwriting all along and has been writing his own chapters back at him. At the festival's closing lantern ceremony, Noor finally says the rehearsed sentence aloud, and they choose each other over the orchard, selling it together to the community that tended it.
about_author: Marguerite Pemberton is the pen name of a former orchard bookkeeper who spent fifteen years cataloguing other families' harvests before writing her own. She lives between two coasts and believes every love story is a land dispute at heart.

chapters.title: The Ghost in the Margins
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In a rented apartment above a bakery, Noor finishes a chapter of Elias Vane's bestselling memoir without ever having been credited on any of his own work. A lawyer's letter arrives: an aunt neither expected has died, leaving a jointly deeded orchard. The beat is quiet dread—his invisible life is about to be made visible.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Deed
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He arrives at Hollow Orchard expecting to sign away his half and finds Elias waiting on the porch, furious and familiar. Neither will sell without the other; the deed requires mutual consent or a full year of joint stewardship. The emotional beat is the shock of recognition and the first flare of old resentment.

chapters.title: What the Trees Remember
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias surveys the neglected rows, remembering the summer all three of them—the aunt included—worked this land before Noor vanished. He agrees to the year only to spite Noor, but assigns him the worst task: reviving the heirloom block. The beat is grief disguised as anger.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Working shoulder to shoulder, they fall into old rhythms—bickering, sharing thermoses, finishing each other's sentences about grafting. Noor hides that he knows Elias's memoir by heart, literally. The beat is reluctant warmth rekindling under the cover of labor.

chapters.title: The Rival's Manuscript
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias discovers Noor's annotated draft pages in the farmhouse attic—proof Noor has been his anonymous ghostwriter for years. Instead of confronting him, Elias begins leaving handwritten replies in the margins. The beat is vertigo: intimacy through paper, betrayal braided with tenderness.

chapters.title: Frost Warning
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. An unseasonal frost threatens the blossom; the town rallies to save the crop, and Noor, who never belonged anywhere, is handed a torch like he's always been one of them. Elias almost says something real by the fire, then retreats. The beat is belonging arriving before either man is ready for it.

chapters.title: Marginalia
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Noor finally reads the margin replies and realizes Elias has known everything—the ghostwriting, the decade-old departure, the reason—and answered with forgiveness Noor can't accept. They fight on the porch about who abandoned whom. The beat is the truth cracking them open at the worst possible time.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. With the memoir's publication announced for festival weekend and a developer circling the orchard, Noor rehearses the sentence he's carried for ten years and keeps failing to say. Elias announces he'll sell his half alone. The beat is despair sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Lantern Night
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At the closing ceremony, Elias publicly dedicates the memoir's final chapter to 'the ghost who wrote me whole.' Before the crowd, before the lanterns rise, Noor says the sentence: 'I left because I loved you, and I've been coming back ever since.' The beat is the climax—vulnerability as public act.

chapters.title: Graft
chapters.summary: Shared POV. They decline the developer, deed the orchard to a community land trust, and stay on as its stewards—not as penance but as choice. The final scene mirrors the first: two names on one document, this time signed willingly. The beat is resolution: inheritance redefined as belonging, love as the thing you stay for.
